meta.title: "It didn't work once, so it will never work" — why your child limits themselves | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to stop drawing conclusions about themselves from a single attempt and give themselves another chance. Game-based course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: "It didn't work once, so it will never work!" — and your child has already written themselves off?
hero.subheadline: One episode isn't a rule. But the brain rushes to close the case. And the child limits themselves before they've even really tried.

media.alt: A child who decides after one failure that something isn't for them

pain.title: "It didn't work" is one result — not a verdict
pain.body:
Didn't answer in class — "I can't do it". Lost a game — "I'm not good enough". Something went wrong — "that's just not for me". At school, in sport, in friendships. One episode becomes "the truth about me" — and the child stops trying.

This isn't giving up quickly or weakness. It's the brain working naturally: it tries to draw a fast conclusion and move on. But one time isn't a rule. A real conclusion takes repetition, testing, experience.

The result — the child limits themselves before they've genuinely tried. "Not for me", "I can't", "it won't work" — labels they put on themselves, and they tend to stick.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 40 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Catches "always/never" conclusions drawn from a single event
🧠 Tells one result apart from a truth about themselves
💬 Questions "that's not for me" and gives themselves another chance
🛡️ Doesn't label themselves after a first failure

social_proof.quote: My daughter lost a tournament and said "I'll never win". A month after the course she said: "That was just one time. I'll try again." I couldn't believe what I was hearing.
social_proof.author: Liudmyla, mum of 9-year-old Nastia

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
